n: In this session we will examine the misconduct of medical workers. In society, relationships between people, including in professional activity, are governed by model social norms. The activity of medical workers is likewise defined by law and other regulatory documents. The session covers professional offences, misconduct and crime, medical error, accident, iatrogenesis and criminal liability.

First, let us distinguish moral norms from legal norms. Moral norms arise in a "natural" way and consist of ethics, religious requirements and customs. Compliance with them is ensured by the force of public opinion. Legal norms, by contrast, are introduced by the state and apply equally to everyone. Compliance with them is ensured by state coercion. That is, in the first case the main force is public opinion, in the second it is state coercion.

Official documents made up of legal norms are called normative legal acts; they are either a law or a subordinate act. Subordinate acts include decrees, resolutions and orders of the President, resolutions and orders of the government, and orders of local authorities. In health care these are the orders, instructions, rules and regulations of the Ministry of Health. This means that medical activity is regulated by a multi-level system of documents.

Failure to meet, or improper performance of, the established requirements in medical activity is called professional offences of medical workers, abbreviated POMW. According to legal theory, an offence has five features. The first is the act, that is, an action or an omission. Then social danger, that is, danger to society. The third is unlawfulness, that is, contradiction of the law. The fourth is fault, that is, intent or negligence. The last is adverse consequences, that is, harm caused.

t: The difference between misconduct and crime
n: By the feature of social danger, a POMW may take the form of misconduct or crime. If an unlawful act does not have the feature of social danger and is not provided for in the Criminal Code, it is called misconduct. Where signs of social danger are present, the act is assessed as a crime. Remember: the distinguishing criterion is the feature of social danger.

From the legal point of view, the misconduct of medical workers is divided into disciplinary, administrative and civil types. In disciplinary misconduct, the established order of work, service and production is violated. An administrative offence relates mainly to a violation of the order of managing an institution. Civil misconduct means a violation of the property and non-property rights of citizens and organisations. That is, we distinguish all three types by what exactly is being violated.

Besides misconduct, there is also a group of adverse outcomes called medical error and accident. The important point is that medical error and accident are not legal concepts. They do not appear in legal literature or legislative documents. Misconduct, however, may be disciplinary, administrative or civil. For this reason we will consider these two concepts separately from misconduct.

Errare humanum est, that is, in Latin: to err is human. The activity of medical workers is no exception. In practice, being entirely free of error is extremely difficult. There are different, sometimes opposing, opinions on how to assess a medical error. It is not acceptable to include most shortcomings, or crime and misconduct, in the category of error.

t: N. I. Pirogov and open disclosure of errors
n: The phrase "medical error" was first proposed by N. I. Pirogov. In 1837 he regarded speaking openly about one's activity and its results as a sacred duty. Pirogov stressed that a doctor has the right to make mistakes, but has no right to conceal them. This means that disclosing an error was considered the doctor's professional duty.

In 1928 I. V. Davidovsky gave a definition of medical error: a medical error is a doctor's conscientious mistake. The causes cited were the imperfection of medical science and methods, an atypical course of the disease, or inadequate training of the doctor. Such an error contains no elements of callousness, carelessness or medical negligence. That is, once these elements appear, we are no longer speaking of a conscientious mistake.

Davidovsky paid particular attention to eliminating errors in the work of other doctors by studying and analysing them. His definition dates from 1928. The first clinico-anatomical conference, however, was held on 9 December 1930 at the Medsantrud hospital in Moscow. Thus the practice of analysing errors together began with that conference.

From the legal standpoint, "medical error" should not mean cases where there was a crime or an administrative, disciplinary or civil misconduct. Adverse consequences resulting from a "conscientious mistake" should logically not entail legal liability. At the same time, they must be disclosed and discussed among colleagues so that they are not repeated. The chain is as follows: conscientious mistake, no legal liability arises, the error is disclosed, and it is discussed among colleagues.

Now let us analyse a case of atypical infarction. A man of about 30 presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and a single episode of loose stool. Blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg, pulse 90 per minute. Suspecting food poisoning, the doctor decided to perform gastric lavage. During insertion of the tube the patient suddenly died. At autopsy, acute myocardial infarction, abdominal form, was found. The history and the atypical course caused the doctor's mistake.

This historical case dates from 1870. In St Petersburg, A. Ya. Krassovsky removed an ovarian cyst; the young woman died 40 hours later. At the pathological examination, N. M. Rudnev found that a sponge tampon had been left in the abdominal cavity, which could have been one of the causes of death. Krassovsky considered it his duty to set out this case openly in the journal Medical Bulletin, 1870, No. 1.

Krassovsky studied such questions as when and how the sponge got into the abdominal cavity and whether measures had been taken to remove it in good time. In his conclusion he proposed recommendations to prevent complications; they have not lost their importance to this day. The recommendation is as follows: count the sponges before and after the operation and attach long tapes to them. That is, the analysis of a single error became a rule preventing complications.

Another historical case dates from 1886. S. P. Kolomnin operated on a wound of a woman's rectum; for anaesthesia he used cocaine by enema, 4 times 6 grains, that is, 1.5 g. About 45 min after the operation her condition deteriorated sharply, and she died after 3 hours; cocaine poisoning was confirmed. Tuberculosis was not confirmed, the patient had syphilis; there had been no indication for the operation at all.

An accident is an adverse outcome resulting from chance circumstances that do not depend on the medical worker and that could be neither foreseen nor prevented. In most cases such an outcome occurs as a result of individual characteristics of organs that were not detected during life. Remember: the main feature is that the medical worker could neither foresee nor prevent it.

Examples of accident. The first is idiosyncrasy to certain ordinary medicines, or the later appearance of hypersensitivity to previously taken drugs. The second is rupture, during an ordinary procedure, of a previously undetected, asymptomatic aneurysm of the cerebral vessels. The third is reflex cardiac arrest during angiography or gastrofibroscopy. The fourth is sudden death from psycho-emotional shock on the eve of an operation.

In an accident, harm to the patient's health or death results from unexpected, unforeseeable chance circumstances. Unlike medical error, an accident does not depend on the doctor's action or omission. Therefore an accident does not entail any liability of the medical worker. However, it must in any case be studied and analysed within the institution. A medical error is likewise studied within the institution.

The term "iatrogenesis" was proposed in 1925 by the German psychiatrist O. Bumke. The term derives from the Greek iatros, a doctor, and gennao, I bring forth. For a long time, iatrogenesis was understood as diseases arising from the adverse effect of a doctor's words or actions on the patient's psyche. In 1970 I. A. Kassirsky proposed including in the concept the incorrect performance of procedures and the incorrect use of medicines.

In some cases iatrogenesis may be caused not by a doctor but by a mid-level medical worker. In 1972 the Hungarian psychotherapist I. Hardy proposed the term "sororigenesis" for adverse consequences of nurses' actions. The term derives from the Latin soror, a sister, or nurse. Thus sororigenesis is the form of iatrogenesis caused by a mid-level medical worker.

Definitions of iatrogenesis differ. Some authors include in it all professional offences, others only negligence, and some regard it as a medical error. An acceptable definition was given by Sergeev and Erofeev in 1998: iatrogenesis is the causing of harm to a patient's health in connection with diagnosis, treatment, prevention or rehabilitation. The current generally accepted interpretation is this: a new pathological condition arising under the influence of medical factors.

t: Medical factor and types of iatrogenesis
n: A medical factor is all the elements of medical technology, that is, diagnosis, treatment, prevention and rehabilitation, as well as the conditions of the institution where the patient is. Types of iatrogenesis: diagnostic, therapeutic, psycho-emotional and informational, preventive, non-treatment and others. Therapeutic iatrogenesis includes medicinal, surgical and physical types. Non-treatment means seeking medical help late.

All adverse consequences arising from professional offences can be interpreted as manifestations of iatrogenesis. They include crime, misconduct, medical error and accident. That is, iatrogenesis is a broad concept that unites these four conditions.

The most serious form of professional offence by medical workers is crime. The features of crime are danger to society, criminal unlawfulness, guilt and the provision of punishment. A socially dangerous act amounts to a criminal offence only when the law classifies it as a crime. Guilt takes the form of intent or negligence, and punishment is provided for.

A person who commits an act intentionally or through negligence may be found guilty; this is stated in Article 20 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Uzbekistan. In direct intent, the person is aware of the danger of the act, foresees its consequences and desires their occurrence. In indirect intent, the person foresees the consequences and consciously allows them to occur; this is Article 21 of the Criminal Code. That is, the difference is that in the first case the consequence is desired, and in the second it is consciously allowed.

There are two kinds of negligence. In overconfidence, the person, knowing that consequences are possible, does not observe precautions and groundlessly hopes they will not occur. In carelessness, the person did not foresee the consequences, although he should and could have foreseen them; this is Article 22 of the Criminal Code. In most cases medical workers are held liable for a crime committed through negligence.

Examples of negligence. On duty, a surgeon and an anaesthetist, without objective reasons, without preparation, and without an assistant or a theatre nurse, performed an elective operation. This is overconfidence. In the second example, the doctor did not ensure the requirements of the standards, and a complication led to death. The doctor should have known the standards, but was not familiar with them. This is carelessness.

t: Circumstances excluding criminality of an act
n: Circumstances excluding the criminality of an act include justified professional risk and extreme necessity. Extreme necessity is set out in Article 38 of the Criminal Code: if the danger cannot be averted by other means, and the harm caused is less than the harm prevented, it is not a crime. Example: outside an institution, in laryngospasm, a tracheostomy was made with improvised means. Life was saved, and purulent complications followed.

Justified risk is defined in Article 41 of the Criminal Code. Risk is considered justified if the action corresponds to modern scientific knowledge and experience, the aim cannot be achieved without risk, and measures are taken to prevent harm. In justified risk, even if a socially useful result is not achieved, no liability arises for the harm caused. Exception: a risk taken in the knowledge that people may die or that grave consequences are possible is not considered justified.

Case analysis: cardiac injury. A patient with a penetrating stab wound of the chest and signs of internal and external bleeding arrived at a district hospital; cardiac injury was identified. There were no special facilities, no possibility of transport, and no possibility of calling a cardiac surgeon in time. The surgeon on duty decided to operate to suture the heart. The decision endangered the patient's life, but it was the only way to save it. The risk was justified, and the act is not a crime.

Criminal liability applies to sane natural persons, as established by the Criminal Code. In most cases these are persons who had reached the age of 16 at the time of committing the crime; this is Article 17 of the Criminal Code. In insanity there is a medical criterion: mental illness, temporary mental disorder, mental deficiency. The legal criterion is the inability to appreciate the significance of one's actions or to control them.

The features of a criminal act established by law are called the elements of a crime. The object is usually the health and life of citizens. The objective side consists of the act, the consequence, the causal link, place, time and method. The subject is a natural person: more often a doctor, in some cases a mid-level or junior worker or an official. The subjective side is fault, motive and purpose.

t: Groups of crimes by medical workers
n: Crimes by medical workers are divided into three groups. Against health and life: negligent homicide, 102; bodily injury, 104, 105, 109, 111; spreading AIDS, 113; abortion, 114; failure to perform a duty, 116; endangerment, 117. Against the family and morality: substitution of a child, 124; disclosure of the secret of adoption, 125; removal of human tissues and organs, 133. Against the order of administration: official negligence, 207; official forgery, 209; taking a bribe, 210; giving a bribe, 211.

t: Article 116 of the Criminal Code: improper performance
n: Article 116 of the Criminal Code is devoted to improper performance of a duty. If failure to perform a professional duty through carelessness or dishonesty causes bodily harm of moderate severity or grave harm, criminal liability arises. Under the second part, if a person obliged to give help does not give it without a valid reason and causes bodily harm of moderate severity or grave harm, the punishment is more severe. If negligence causes the death of people or other graver consequences, a still more severe punishment is established.

According to Article 30 of the law, medical and pharmaceutical workers are obliged to provide emergency care regardless of place and time. Valid objective reasons: the worker's illness, being occupied with helping a more seriously ill patient, absence of medicines, instruments and transport, a natural disaster threatening life. Not considered valid reasons: days off and holidays, time outside working hours, leave, lack of specialised knowledge, personal enmity towards the patient.

According to I. G. Vermel, 1988, three conditions are needed for liability even when an adverse outcome has occurred. First: the action is objectively wrong and contrary to the instruction and standard. Second: given his qualification, the worker realises it is wrong and is able to make the right decision. Third: the action or omission stands in a direct causal link with a serious adverse outcome. The same conditions are also required for civil liability.

t: Criminal abortion (Article 114 of the Criminal Code)
n: Criminal abortion is provided for in Article 114 of the Criminal Code. Under the first part, an obstetrician or gynaecologist is liable if he performs an abortion outside an institution or where it is medically not possible. The second part concerns a person who has no right to carry out artificial termination of pregnancy and does so. Permitted terms: at the woman's wish, up to 12 weeks; on social indication, up to 22 weeks; on medical indication, irrespective of term.

The operation is performed only by an obstetrician-gynaecologist in a specialised institution in the established manner; a mid-level worker or a person without medical education cannot perform it. Contraindications: a term of more than 12 weeks, acute infectious diseases, acute inflammation of the genital organs, purulent foci, less than 6 months since the last abortion. Grave bodily harm falls under Article 104, while the woman's death and loss of the ability to bear children fall under the third paragraph of Article 114. If the woman does it herself, or in a state of necessity, there is no liability.

Let us summarise. A POMW may be misconduct or crime. Medical error and accident are not legal concepts, and a conscientious mistake should not entail liability. All adverse consequences can be interpreted within the framework of iatrogenesis; an accident, however, does not depend on the doctor's actions. Criminal liability arises only when a socially dangerous act is committed intentionally or through negligence.
